text: Autonomy (ethical). The characteristic of a moral being in virtue of which he is said to be a 'law to himself'; not in the sense of following his desires, but because the law which he recognizes as morally binding upon him is the law laid down by his own moral consciousness. ( W.R.S .) In this sense the term is used by Kant, Grundl . d . Met . d . Sitten , ii; Krit , d . prakt . Vernunft , I. i. I, §§ 7, 8. He distinguishes between the true or rational self and the natural self with its content of sense and desire. This true self, which is practical reason, is at the same time will, and determines itself by its own law, which is the moral law. In other passages, however, it should be remembered (e.g. Krit . d . prakt . Vernunft , 229-31, ed. Rosenkranz), empirical character is referred to the 'causality of the noumenon.' All other ethical systems, inasmuch as they rely upon a law or end outside the rational will, are classed by him as systems of Heteronomy. ( W.R.S . - H.S .)
